Let's extract needed info:

Motivation: survey emerging field of RFMs, need for generalist core for cobots, gap between hardware and robust models, need for adaptable low-effort intelligence for high-mix low-volume industrial settings. Sources S1 and S2.

Assessment method: build three corpora (primary RFM set 1025 works, industrial-implication set 125, auxiliary 113) using automated pipeline (ASQS, duplicate removal, LLM relevance filtering, manual enrichment). Derive 11 industrial requirements mapped to 47 attributes, 149-item criteria catalogue. Apply via GPT-5.1 pipeline to 324 manipulation-capable RFMs, yielding 48,276 binary decisions, compute scores. Scores normalized, overall score 0.12, peak I1 0.44. Also mention that scores are proportional, no empirical data, lack confidence intervals. Sources S1 and S2.

Main findings: top model Gemini Robotics 1.5 only satisfies about one-tenth of criteria (overall 0.12), high breadth but shallow depth, strong on adaptability, benchmarking, data usage, low on safety, HRI, real-time latency, cost. Overall low maturity across corpus, most models near zero on many criteria, only I1 common. No model meets all criteria. Research concentrates on adaptability/flexibility, benchmarking, data usage; safety/compliance, HRI, real-time, cost underrepresented. Need for layered architectures, better benchmarks, evaluation protocols. Sources S1 and S2.

Limitations: structure not reliably reconstructed, tables missing, scores are automatically generated, lack external validation, represent indirect estimates not measured capabilities. Unreported model capabilities (e.g., safety, real-time) lead to near-zero scores because not captured; assessment limited to reported attributes. Scope of expert validation is limited; authors note lack of external validation, expert review. Also extraction warning about unreliable reconstruction. Sources S1 and S2.

Unreported model capabilities affect assessment: because the pipeline relies on documented attributes; missing info leads to zero/near-zero scores, skewing assessment; indicates need for expert validation to fill gaps. Scope of expert validation: limited, as authors stress that ratings are context-dependent, automatically generated, lack external validation, thus expert validation is narrow.

Appendix A: curated bibliography of 55 recent surveys (2023-2025) covering vision-language-action models, LLMs, multimodal foundations, applications; serves as reference map, no quantitative data. [S2]

Appendix C: defines industrial-implication rubric in detail; eight primary categories expanded with benchmark themes; outlines safety, robustness, compliance, real-time, cost, explainability requirements. [S2]

Appendix D: presents RFM overview; each of 324 RFMs gets proportional industrial applicability scores across eleven dimensions; scores normalized; shows low totals; confirms fragmented applicability. [S2]
